summary: This RFC describes two methods of encapsulating IP datagrams on an IEEE 802.3 network and asks for discussion. It was replaced by RFC 1042.

eli5.summary: Two ways to put Internet letters inside Ethernet-style envelopes. Later a single recipe replaced this note.

questions: how to send ip over ieee 802.3
subtitle: Two methods for encapsulating IP on IEEE 802.3 local area networks

tldr.problem: When IEEE 802.3 networks began to be used, there was no standard way to send IP datagrams over them, yet existing Ethernet-style networks were already doing it in a non-standard way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes two encapsulation methods: one compatible with existing Ethernet IP transmission, and another following the IEEE 802.2/802.3 standard more strictly. Both map IP addresses to 802.3 physical addresses using either static tables or a protocol similar to ARP.
tldr.outcome: The 802.2/802.3 compatible method was recommended as preferable for new installations, but the Ethernet-compatible method was allowed to coexist during transition. RFC 1042 later superseded this with a single unified standard.

today: RFC 948 is Historic. It was superseded by RFC 1042, which unified the methods for IP transmission over IEEE 802 networks.

sections.title: Introduction to IEEE 802 and Ethernet
sections.content:
The IEEE 802 project defined a family of standards for local area networks covering Physical and Data Link layers. Physical layer standards include 802.3 (based on Ethernet), 802.4, and 802.5, while the 802.2 standard covers the Logical Link Control sublayer. Although 802.3 shares physical layer compatibility with Ethernet Version 2.0, their data link layers differ significantly, creating a problem for IP transmission.

Many installations already transmitted IP datagrams using the Ethernet-compatible method from RFC 894. This RFC explores how to add 802.3 Physical Layer compatible connections to existing networks without violating the 802.3 standard.
sections.eli5: Ethernet and 802.3 are very similar but differ in how they label what goes inside. This note explains two ways to make them work together.

sections.title: Ethernet Compatible Method
sections.content:
The Ethernet compatible method relies on a loophole in the 802.3 standard. The 802.3 packet header includes a field that Ethernet uses as a protocol type field, but 802.3 defines it as a length field. The maximum allowed length value is 1500 octets. Since packets with length values greater than 1500 can be ignored or used privately, the field can be reused as a protocol type field when the protocol numbers are greater than 1500.

IP, ARP, and trailer encapsulation protocol numbers all exceed 1500, so the Ethernet compatible method from RFC 894 works unchanged on IEEE 802.3 networks at 10 megabits per second.
sections.eli5: The 802.3 label field has room for a secret: if the number is bigger than 1500, it secretly means something else, like a protocol type.

sections.title: IEEE 802.2/802.3 Compatible Method
sections.content:
The preferred method follows the 802.2/802.3 standards strictly. IP datagrams are transmitted in standard 802.2 LLC Type 1 Unnumbered Information format, with the DSAP and SSAP fields of the 802.2 header both set to 96 (the IEEE-assigned global Service Access Point for IP). The data field contains the IP header followed directly by the IP data.

When the 802.3 packet is smaller than the standard minimum frame size, the data field is padded with zero octets to meet the size requirement. This padding is not part of the IP packet and does not count toward the IP header's total length field.
sections.eli5: The 802.3 way puts the IP message in a standard labeled box with clear rules about size and structure.

sections.title: Address Mapping
sections.content:
The 32-bit Internet address must be mapped to a 48-bit or 16-bit 802.3 physical address. The RFC describes two approaches: a static table where each host knows all other hosts' Internet and 802.3 addresses, or a dynamic discovery procedure similar to the Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (ARP).

The broadcast Internet address (all ones in the host part) should map to the broadcast 802.3 address (all binary ones). The RFC strongly recommends using ARP-like dynamic discovery rather than static tables.
sections.eli5: You need to know which envelope address (802.3) corresponds to which Internet address. You can look it up in a list, or ask the network on the fly.

sections.title: Transition and Conclusion
sections.content:
The two encapsulation methods can coexist on the same local area network, but this partitions the network into incompatible subnetworks. A single host could support both methods and act as a gateway, but this introduces significant performance penalties and should be avoided.

The 802.2/802.3 compatible method is preferable because IEEE 802.2 and 802.3 have been accepted nationally and internationally, and the same method works with other IEEE 802 Physical Layer implementations. However, controlled transition from existing Ethernet installations is necessary. New implementations should allow a static choice of encapsulation methods, and existing implementations should be modified to provide this choice. During transition, all hosts would use the Ethernet compatible method, then switch to the 802.2/802.3 method once all implementations support it.
sections.eli5: Use the new standard way on new machines. For old machines still talking to new machines, you can run both methods for a while, but eventually everyone should use the same new way.
